why_use_this:
Most matrices that show up in real graph, PDE, and large-linear-system code are mostly zeros -- a graph's adjacency matrix has one entry per edge, not one per pair of nodes; a finite-difference/finite-element discretization matrix has a handful of nonzero entries per row, not one per grid point in the whole domain. Storing that as a dense `Vec<f64>` of length `n_rows * n_cols` (what [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix) does) wastes memory and time proportional to the *zeros* you're not using -- both memory and every operation's cost scale as `O(n^2)`/`O(n^3)` regardless of how sparse the real data is. Reach for vani-sparse instead of vani-matrix once your matrix's nonzero count (`nnz`) is much smaller than `n_rows * n_cols`: every operation here costs roughly `O(nnz)` instead, so a matrix too large to even allocate densely can still be built (via `SparseCOO`) and operated on (via `SparseCSR`) in the format built for exactly this shape of data. If you're not sure whether your matrix is sparse enough to bother, `sparse_csr_nnz(m)` compared against `m.n_rows * m.n_cols` answers that directly.

One running example threads through every function's math note below, so you can watch the SAME matrix move through each operation instead of re-orienting to a new example each time:

\[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \]

Stored in CSR form, `A` has only 4 nonzero entries: \((0,0)\!\to\!2\), \((1,2)\!\to\!3\), \((2,0)\!\to\!1\), \((2,2)\!\to\!5\) -- the other 5 of its 9 entries are zero and are never stored at all. That's the entire idea this package is built around: every operation below only ever touches those 4 numbers, never the 5 zeros.

sparse_csr_matvec.intuition: Think of matrix-vector multiplication row by row: row \(i\) of the matrix tells you exactly how to combine the numbers in \(x\) to produce \(y_i\). If most of a row is zero, most of those "instructions" are just "ignore this entry of \(x\) completely." A dense matvec still walks past every one of those ignore-me zeros, multiplying by 0 and adding 0 for nothing. A sparse matvec skips them outright -- it never even looks at the columns a row doesn't have an entry for.
sparse_csr_matvec.formula: \[ y = Ax, \qquad y_i = \sum_{j} A_{ij}\,x_j \] but the sum only ever runs over the nonzero \(j\)'s of row \(i\) (the ones actually stored in `col_idx`/`vals` between `row_ptr[i]` and `row_ptr[i+1]`), not every \(j\) from \(0\) to \(n_{\text{cols}}-1\).
sparse_csr_matvec.example:
Using the running example \(A\) from the top of this page, let \(x = (1,\,2,\,3)\). Compute \(y=Ax\) one row at a time, using ONLY each row's stored nonzero entries:

- Row 0 has one nonzero entry: column 0, value 2. So \(y_0 = 2 \cdot x_0 = 2\cdot 1 = 2\). (Columns 1 and 2 are skipped entirely -- not multiplied by zero, just never visited.)
- Row 1 has one nonzero entry: column 2, value 3. So \(y_1 = 3\cdot x_2 = 3\cdot 3 = 9\).
- Row 2 has two nonzero entries: column 0 (value 1) and column 2 (value 5). So \(y_2 = 1\cdot x_0 + 5\cdot x_2 = 1\cdot1 + 5\cdot3 = 1+15 = 16\).

So \(y = (2,\,9,\,16)\) -- exactly what you'd get multiplying the full \(3\times3\) matrix out by hand, but this computation only ever touched 4 numbers (the 4 stored nonzeros), never the 5 zeros.
sparse_csr_matvec.why: For a small \(3\times3\) example the saving looks trivial -- 4 multiplications instead of 9. But the SHAPE of the saving is what matters: dense matvec always costs \(n_{\text{rows}}\cdot n_{\text{cols}}\) multiplications no matter what the matrix contains, while sparse matvec costs exactly `nnz`. For a million-row matrix with only 5 nonzero entries per row (extremely common for graphs and PDE grids), that's the difference between 5 million operations and several trillion -- not a constant-factor speedup, a difference in which problems are even tractable to compute at all.

sparse_csr_matmul.intuition: Matrix-matrix multiplication is just matrix-vector multiplication done once per OUTPUT row, where each output row is a weighted combination of the SECOND matrix's rows. Gustavson's algorithm makes this concrete: to build output row \(i\), look at which columns row \(i\) of \(A\) has nonzero entries in -- each one names a row of \(B\) to pull in, scaled by that entry's value -- and add all those scaled rows of \(B\) together.
sparse_csr_matmul.formula: \[ C = AB, \qquad C_{i,:} \;=\; \sum_{k \,\in\, \text{nz}(A_{i,:})} A_{ik}\cdot B_{k,:} \] where \(\text{nz}(A_{i,:})\) means "the column indices where row \(i\) of \(A\) has a nonzero entry." Each output row is accumulated into a dense length-\(n_{\text{cols}}\) scratch buffer, then reset before the next row starts.
sparse_csr_matmul.example:
Take \(C = A \cdot A\) using the running-example \(A\) from the top of this page (multiplying \(A\) by itself, so you only need to keep track of one matrix):

- Row 0 of \(A\) has one nonzero: column 0, value 2. So \(C_{0,:} = 2 \cdot A_{0,:} = 2\cdot(2,0,0) = (4,0,0)\) -- pull in row 0 of \(A\), scaled by 2.
- Row 1 of \(A\) has one nonzero: column 2, value 3. So \(C_{1,:} = 3 \cdot A_{2,:} = 3\cdot(1,0,5) = (3,0,15)\) -- pull in row 2 of \(A\) (not row 1!), scaled by 3, since row 1's only nonzero points at column 2.
- Row 2 of \(A\) has two nonzeros: column 0 (value 1) and column 2 (value 5). So \(C_{2,:} = 1\cdot A_{0,:} + 5\cdot A_{2,:} = (2,0,0) + (5,0,25) = (7,0,25)\) -- two of \(A\)'s rows get pulled in and added together.

So \(A\cdot A = \begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\3&0&15\\7&0&25\end{pmatrix}\). Notice row 2's computation is exactly what the formula above describes: two terms, one per nonzero column in \(A\)'s row 2, each term an entire scaled row of the other matrix.
sparse_csr_matmul.why: The dense-accumulator reset costs \(O(n_{\text{cols}})\) per output row regardless of sparsity, so this implementation is \(O(n_{\text{rows}}\cdot n_{\text{cols}})\) just for the resets on top of the genuinely sparse accumulation work -- worth knowing if you're multiplying a matrix with very many rows against a very wide result; see the README's Gustavson's-algorithm note for the (not yet implemented) merge-based alternative that would avoid this.

sparse_csr_add.intuition: Adding two sparse matrices entrywise only needs to do real work where at least ONE of the two matrices has a nonzero entry -- a position that's zero in both inputs is trivially zero in the sum too, and never needs to be visited. So this walks each row of both matrices side by side (both are sorted by column already), merging as it goes: matching columns get summed, a column that appears in only one input just copies through unchanged.
sparse_csr_add.formula: \[ C = A + B, \qquad C_{ij} = A_{ij} + B_{ij} \] computed by merging each row's sorted \((\text{col\_idx}, \text{val})\) pairs from \(A\) and \(B\) the same way merging two sorted lists works.
sparse_csr_add.example:
Using the running-example \(A\), add a second small matrix \(B = \begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&5&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}\). Merge row by row:

- Row 0: \(A\) has column 0 (value 2); \(B\) has column 2 (value 1). No columns match, so both just copy through: row 0 of \(C\) is \((2,0,1)\).
- Row 1: \(A\) has column 2 (value 3); \(B\) has column 1 (value 5). No match again: row 1 of \(C\) is \((0,5,3)\).
- Row 2: \(A\) has columns 0 (value 1) and 2 (value 5); \(B\) has column 0 (value 1). Column 0 MATCHES between the two, so those sum: \(1+1=2\) at column 0. Column 2 only appears in \(A\), so it copies through as 5. Row 2 of \(C\) is \((2,0,5)\).

So \(C = A+B = \begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\0&5&3\\2&0&5\end{pmatrix}\) -- and notice the ONLY place any actual addition happened was row 2, column 0, the one position where both inputs had a stored entry.
sparse_csr_add.why: This is why the merge approach beats "convert both to dense, add, convert back to sparse": the work done is proportional to how many nonzero POSITIONS exist across both inputs combined, never to the matrices' full \(n_{\text{rows}}\times n_{\text{cols}}\) size -- for two very sparse matrices, that's a dramatically smaller number.

sparse_csr_transpose.intuition: Transposing swaps the meaning of "row" and "column" for every entry -- a value that used to say "I'm in row 2, column 0" now says "I'm in row 0, column 2" instead. For a sparse matrix, that's ALL there is to it: take every stored \((\text{row}, \text{col}, \text{val})\) triple and swap row and col. The only extra work is that CSR requires each row to be sorted by column, so after swapping, the new rows need re-sorting -- swapping can easily scramble the order.
sparse_csr_transpose.example: Using the running-example \(A\), its four stored entries are \((0,0)\!\to\!2\), \((1,2)\!\to\!3\), \((2,0)\!\to\!1\), \((2,2)\!\to\!5\). Swap row and column on each one: \((0,0)\!\to\!2\) stays \((0,0)\!\to\!2\) (a diagonal entry never moves), \((1,2)\!\to\!3\) becomes \((2,1)\!\to\!3\), \((2,0)\!\to\!1\) becomes \((0,2)\!\to\!1\), and \((2,2)\!\to\!5\) stays \((2,2)\!\to\!5\). Collecting those by their NEW row: row 0 now has entries at columns 0 and 2 (values 2 and 1); row 1 now has an entry at column 1 (value 3); row 2 still has just its own diagonal entry (value 5). So \[ A^T = \begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\0&0&3\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}. \] Reading straight across confirms it: \(A^T\)'s row 0 is \(A\)'s COLUMN 0, which was \((2,0,1)\) reading down -- matches.
sparse_csr_transpose.why: Notice \(A\) had nonzero entries scattered across rows 0, 1, and 2, but only 1 nonzero in column 1 across the whole matrix (none, actually -- column 1 is entirely zero in \(A\)) -- after transposing, that becomes ROW 1 of \(A^T\) being nearly empty. A sparse matrix's row-sparsity pattern and column-sparsity pattern can look completely different, which is exactly why this function has real work to do (re-sorting) rather than being a free relabeling.

sparse_csr_scale.intuition: Scaling every entry by a constant \(s\) is the one operation that can never change WHICH entries are nonzero (as long as \(s \ne 0\)) -- a stored value just becomes a bigger or smaller version of itself, and anything that was already zero (and not stored) stays zero. So this is the simplest possible sparse operation: walk the stored values once, multiply each by \(s\), leave the row/column structure completely untouched.
sparse_csr_scale.example: Using the running-example \(A\) and \(s=2\): each of the 4 stored values doubles. \((0,0)\!\to\!2\) becomes \((0,0)\!\to\!4\), \((1,2)\!\to\!3\) becomes \((1,2)\!\to\!6\), \((2,0)\!\to\!1\) becomes \((2,0)\!\to\!2\), and \((2,2)\!\to\!5\) becomes \((2,2)\!\to\!10\). So \[ 2A = \begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&0&6\\2&0&10\end{pmatrix}, \] every entry exactly doubled, and still only 4 nonzero entries -- the same 4 positions as \(A\) itself.
sparse_csr_scale.why: Compare this to `sparse_csr_add`, which had to actually MERGE two rows' worth of column indices: scaling never needs to look at column indices at all, only the stored values -- the cheapest of this package's arithmetic operations, and a useful building block (e.g. computing \(A - B\) as \(A + (-1)\!\cdot\!B\) by composing `sparse_csr_scale` with `sparse_csr_add`).

sparse_csr_diagonal.intuition: The diagonal of a matrix is just "every entry where the row number equals the column number." For a sparse matrix, a diagonal position that was never explicitly stored isn't an error or a missing value -- CSR treats every unstored position as exactly zero, diagonal or not, so an absent diagonal entry simply means that diagonal value IS zero.
sparse_csr_diagonal.example: Using the running-example \(A = \begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&0&3\\1&0&5\end{pmatrix}\): \(d_0 = A_{00} = 2\) (stored). \(d_1 = A_{11}\) -- position (1,1) was never pushed via `sparse_coo_push`, so it's absent, meaning \(d_1 = 0\). \(d_2 = A_{22} = 5\) (stored). So \(d = (2,\,0,\,5)\) -- reading straight down the matrix's own diagonal confirms it directly.
sparse_csr_diagonal.why: This is a small but easy trap for anyone used to dense arrays: don't confuse "not stored" with "error" or "undefined" -- in CSR, absent always means zero, and `sparse_csr_diagonal` (like every other function in this package) relies on that convention rather than treating a missing diagonal entry as a special case to guard against.
